extracted.intended_audience: philosophers of mathematics and mathematicians interested in the nature of mathematical explanation
extracted.subtask_description: Extracts and analyzes criteria for when a mathematical proof or argument counts as an explanation; compares candidate criteria (generality, visualization, discoverability) and advances a central account based on 'characterizing properties' and generalizability via deformation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Characterizing property (central criterion)
rubrics_metrics.description: An explanatory proof makes reference to a 'characterizing property' of an entity or structure mentioned in the theorem — a property unique to that entity within a family or domain — such that it is evident the result depends on that property.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Steiner's principal proposal: the proof should show how the theorem follows from a property that picks out the object in a family (e.g. prime-power expansion for irrationality of sqrt(2); the right triangle as uniquely decomposable for the Pythagorean theorem). From the proof it should be clear that substituting a different object of the same domain will make the theorem fail or change; one should be able to vary the object and see how the theorem responds. The emphasis is on relative/ family-based characterization (the domain/family is left informal but is essential).

rubrics_metrics.name: Generality / abstraction (necessary but not sufficient)
rubrics_metrics.description: Generality or abstraction can contribute to explanatory power (e.g. analytic proofs giving stronger estimates for prime distribution), but mere generality/abstractness by itself does not guarantee explanation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Feferman's and Kreisel's theses that more general or abstract proofs are more explanatory are discussed and rejected as a sole criterion. Examples: analytic proofs of the Prime Number Theorem give stronger quantitative control and so are often seen as more explanatory; but other more-general proofs (Hardy's general proof for nth-root irrationality) may not be more explanatory than a more specific, pictorial proof. Use generality as suggestive evidence, not a conclusive test.

rubrics_metrics.name: Generalizability via deformation (explanatory through families)
rubrics_metrics.description: A proof is explanatory if it is 'generalizable' by varying the characterizing property to obtain a family of related proofs/theorems — i.e. one can 'deform' the proof-idea to produce new, related results.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Key operational test: can we rework the proof, holding the central idea, while substituting related characterizing properties to derive new theorems? If yes, the proof is explanatory. Steiner contrasts this with mere abstraction: explanatory proofs are those that can be deformed to yield a systematic array of theorems (e.g. proofs using prime-power expansion generalize to results about pth roots; combinatorial diagram arguments generalize to classes of partition identities).

rubrics_metrics.name: Visualization / pictorialness (common symptom)
rubrics_metrics.description: Proofs that are visualizable or have a clear pictorial representation often feel explanatory (e.g. geometric proof of sum 1+...+n or pictorial partition arguments for Euler identities).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Visualization is a plausible indicator of explanation because it often reveals characterizing properties (symmetry, geometry). Steiner notes it's subjective and not a standalone criterion, but many classical explanatory proofs are pictorial. Use visualization as supportive evidence, recognizing counterexamples where visual proofs may fail to capture the deeper characterizing property.

rubrics_metrics.name: Discoverability (instrument-of-discovery as a symptom, not criterion)
rubrics_metrics.description: The fact that a proof could have been used to discover a theorem (rather than merely verify it) is often correlated with explanatory proofs, but is not a reliable criterion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Steiner gives Euler's parameter-based proof as a counterexample: Euler's proof could serve as a discovery method yet fails to explain the partition identity as well as the combinatorial argument. Treat discoverability as an occasional symptom of explanation, not as a defining standard.

rubrics_metrics.name: Deduction from 'essence' / relevance to behavior
rubrics_metrics.description: An explanatory proof deduces the behavior of the mathematical entity from its 'essence' or characterizing features — showing relevance by linking the theorem to why the object behaves as it does.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explanation should show why the theorem follows from properties that capture the object's nature within an appropriate family (e.g. Euler's V-E+F=2 characterizes the sphere and explains Euclid's result on regular solids; Galois group properties explain solvability in radicals). Emphasize explanatory relevance: the proof should illuminate which features are doing the explanatory work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Partial / cross-domain characterization (weakened characterization allowed)
rubrics_metrics.description: In contemporary mathematics an explanatory link may rely on a partial or indirect characterization in a different domain (e.g. assigning Galois groups or topological invariants) that yields explanatory information about the original object.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Steiner allows weakening 'characterization' to partial characterization: the counterpart in another domain (Galois group, topological invariant) may not uniquely pick out one object but still provides explanatory control over behavior. Guidance: accept explanations that proceed via such cross-domain representations when they reveal why things behave as they do, while noting that uniqueness is not always required.

rubrics_metrics.name: Combinatorial / interpretive enumeration explanations
rubrics_metrics.description: An explanation that links algebraic or analytic identities to combinatorial/interpretive counting properties (e.g. Euler product vs sum interpreted as enumerating partitions) is explanatory because it connects the formula to a characterizing combinatorial structure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Euler's product identity is better explained by showing the product enumerates partitions into odd unequal parts while the series enumerates self-adjoint partitions; the bijective/combinatorial picture exposes the characterizing property and allows deformation to related partition identities. Use combinatorial interpretations to reveal the structural source of a formula.

rubrics_metrics.name: Anti-patterns: mere verification, inductive proofs, or overly formal parameter tricks
rubrics_metrics.description: Proofs that merely verify a theorem without revealing dependence on a characterizing property — including many straightforward inductive proofs and parameterized algebraic manipulations — often fail to be explanatory.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Steiner argues that induction typically 'does not characterize anything mentioned in the theorem' and thus tends not to explain; Euler's analytic/parameter proof, while general and discovery-capable, is judged less explanatory than the combinatorial proof. Use absence of a characterizing property and inability to deform as indicators of non-explanatory proofs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Explanation of behavior (explanations can target families/behavior, not only single theorems)
rubrics_metrics.description: A legitimate mathematical explanation may explain the 'behavior' of an object or class of objects across a range of theorems (e.g. phenomena in recursion theory, Ramanujan-style snapshots), not merely justify a single isolated result.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Steiner emphasizes that explanations sometimes aim to account for patterns or systematic phenomena (why certain analogies hold or break down), and such explanations still fit the characterizing-property model: they show how a property or representation governs the observed behavior. Evaluate such explanations by how well they identify the controlling characterizing features and permit deformation to related cases.
